title: Krishna Summons Garuda at Bhishmaka's House
subtitle: The king of birds appears at a thought, and the assembled kings learn who has come to the swayamvara.
story:
Krishna reached Bhishmaka's house at the hour when the sun, low in the west, turned the colour of heated iron. He had come to see the swayamvara, and what he saw first was the gathering itself: the spacious arena crowded with camps, the tents of a hundred kings filling the plain before Kundina, the smoke of their fires rising into the evening air.

For a moment he was moved by what the verses candidly call a rajasika inclination — a restless stirring of pride, the desire to make the assembled kings understand who had arrived. It was not a sinful impulse, the text is careful to say; it was the wish to display his own prowess. And Krishna had a way of displaying prowess that no king in that arena could match.

He thought of Garuda.

Not a messenger, not a summons — a thought was enough. As soon as Vinata's son was in his mind, the king of birds took a form that could be seen easily and came to Krishna. He came with the strokes of his wings, wings that could agitate even the wind itself, and every man gathered there — kings, warriors, servants, all of them — trembled, bent over, and fell to the earth, writhing like serpents deprived of the power to rise.

Krishna alone stood firm, like a mountain. He knew, before he saw, that the king of birds had arrived. Then he saw him: Garuda, adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, shaking the earth with the flapping of his wings; golden-feathered, bright as a mountain made of minerals; the weapons on his back lying with their faces downward like licking serpents seeking the touch of Vishnu's hand; black serpents dragged in his talons as he came. This was the bird who had brought ambrosia for Krishna, the destroyer of serpents and the terror of the Daityas, whose emblem stood on the flagstaff above Krishna's car — and now he stood before his lord, like a god bringing a gift.

Krishna welcomed him with pleasure. "O foremost of birds, you are welcome," he said. "We are going to the swayamvara at the house of Kaishika — come with us. Hundreds of powerful kings have gathered there with their elephants, horses and cars. We shall behold those high-souled ones."

So the car set out again, with Garuda beside it and the mighty car-warriors of the Yadavas following, and when they reached the city of Vidarbha, all the kings who had come for the swayamvara were filled with delight at the sight of them. Holding all manner of weapons though they were, they hurried to make arrangements for Krishna's quarters, as though the terror of the king of birds had already passed and left only wonder behind.

Bhishmaka himself rose from among the kings and came to welcome him. The king, well read in the moral laws, brought water to wash Krishna's feet and rinse his mouth, offered the ritual arghya, and placed him in his own city. And as Shankara is said to enter the hill Kailasa, Krishna entered with his army the house that had been kept ready for him from before. He was honoured there with edibles and drinks, with jewels and affection, and Vasava's younger brother Krishna lived happily in the house of Bhishmaka.

The kings who had fallen before the king of birds — the same kings who now pressed forward, delighted, to make room for Krishna — had been shown, without a single word of threat, what stood beside him. The swayamvara had not yet begun, and already the assembly knew who had come to it.
reflection: The verses are candid that this is display — a rajasika impulse, pride without sin. Krishna arrives at the swayamvara and announces himself with the king of birds, so that every king in the arena understands, before a word is spoken, who has come. And the scene ends in the quietest possible key: Bhishmaka washing Krishna's feet and honouring him, and Krishna at rest in the house prepared for him.
tradition_note: The Harivamsha names Rukmini's father both Bhishmaka and Kaishika; this retelling follows the title of the episode and uses Bhishmaka throughout.
next_story_tease: But in Bhishmaka's house, Rukmini had her own counsel to give Krishna.
hero_scene: Garuda appearing before Krishna among the encamped kings of the swayamvara — wings shaking the earth, golden feathers bright as a mountain of minerals, black serpents dragged in his talons — while warriors lie fallen and trembling on the ground and Krishna alone stands firm like a mountain.
